query: Research on refractory multicomponent alloys has emphasized exceptional strength at room and elevated temperatures, while mechanical assessment has relied mainly on compression and has included relatively few tensile studies. WFeNiMo fragments released more chemical energy than tungsten-alloy fragments in thin-steel-target penetration tests, and HfZrTiTa0.53 was reported at 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain. This evidence establishes strength and energetic promise but leaves limited tensile ductility, load-bearing reliability, and processability unresolved. Subject to preserving strength and impact-triggered energy release, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention for HfZrTiTa0.53 that could improve tensile ductility and uniform elongation? Include the intervention, causal mechanism, directional or quantitative outcomes relative to the reported baseline, the applicable temperature, loading mode, and strain-rate limits, prior evidence from the cited studies, and matched compression, tension, and impact tests with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Moderate cold deformation (8–15% cold rolling) followed by a controlled sub-transus annealing treatment of HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy refines its grain structure and activates enhanced dislocation slip and potential nanotwinning, thereby increasing tensile ductility and uniform elongation while preserving its high strength and impact-triggered energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy with a reported yield strength of 786 MPa, compressive strength of 1314 MPa, and terminal tensile strain of 13.5% (measured at room temperature under quasi-static loading).
generation.intervention: Apply moderate cold rolling (8–15% reduction) followed by controlled sub-transus annealing designed to achieve a fully recrystallized, ultrafine-grained microstructure.
generation.conditions: Room temperature tensile tests at quasi-static strain rates (approximately 1×10⁻³ s⁻¹), with matched compression and impact tests (including dynamic strain rates for impact energy release), ensuring that the treatment does not adversely affect high-temperature or high-strain-rate performance.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained microstructure with increased grain boundary density that promotes the activation of multiple deformation mechanisms (enhanced dislocation slip, potential nanotwinning) during tensile loading.
generation.mechanism: The refined grain structure elevates the strain-hardening capacity and delays necking by providing additional obstacles to dislocation motion. This results in improved uniform elongation without compromising the intrinsic strength or the energy release characteristics under impact.
generation.predicted_outcome: Increase in uniform elongation from approximately 13.5% to near 25–30% while maintaining yield strength close to 780 MPa and compressive strength near 1314 MPa, along with preserved impact-triggered chemical energy release.
generation.baseline: Original HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy properties: 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal tensile strain at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The intervention must be optimized so that the enhanced ductility does not induce a significant drop in strength or negatively alter the phase stability required for impact-triggered energy release; effectiveness is validated only within room temperature and quasi-static loading conditions.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact quantitative improvement in elongation and the potential trade-offs in strength. Further systematic experiments are needed to verify that the controlled thermomechanical processing does not impair impact energy release.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy samples: one group using the standard processing route (baseline) and a second group subjected to moderate cold rolling (8–15% reduction) followed by controlled sub-transus annealing. Perform a series of mechanical tests, including room temperature tensile tests at a quasi-static strain rate (∼1×10⁻³ s⁻¹), compressive tests, and impact tests to evaluate energy release.
measurements: Uniform elongation (% tensile strain at fracture)
Impact energy release (quantified via standardized impact tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically treated samples fail to show a statistically significant improvement in uniform elongation (i.e., an increase from ~13.5% to at least ~25%) without a reduction in yield or compressive strength exceeding 5–10% of the baseline values, then the hypothesis is falsified.

This study demonstrates that the addition of W significantly enhances the mechanical properties of TiZrMo alloys, with the phase ratio effectively being controlled by adjusting the elemental composition. As a result, a dual-phase Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA was successfully fabricated and subjected to comprehensive quasi-static and dynamic loading experiments to evaluate its energy release capability and mechanical properties for potential structural applications. The Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA demonstrated exceptional quasi-static mechanical performance, with a yield strength of 1490 MPa, an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa, and a fracture strain of 30%. Under dynamic loading at a strain rate of 3000 s−1, the alloy exhibited an even higher ultimate strength of 2300 MPa and maintained a fracture strain of 24%, showcasing its remarkable ability to retain plasticity under extreme conditions. Additionally, the Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA displayed significant chemical energy release and a high energy release capacity. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. Joseph et al. reported that both arc-melted and direct laser sintered Al0.3CoCrFeNi alloy samples (with FCC structure) exhibited a yield strength of 200 MPa, excellent strain hardening, and had tensile failure strain above 1. Li et al. discovered that tensile strength and elongation of the FCC Al0.3CoCrFeNi alloy increased with decreasing temperatures and reached 1010 MPa and 68% at 77 K. The Charpy impact energy of the Al0.3CoCrFeNi alloy was approximately 413 J at room temperature and 328 J at 77 K. This superior ductility and ultrahigh Charpy impact toughness of this alloy are the result of mechanial nanotwinning instead of planar slip dislocations. This has been also observed by Gludovatz et al. in the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy. Deformation-induced nanotwinning delays the onset of necking instability (i.e., localized plastic deformation that can lead to premature failure) to higher strains. In order to understand the strain hardening mechanisms of the Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, it is important to establish the microstructure evolution of deformed samples. Figure 3 shows the room- and cryogenic-temperature engineering stress–strain curves of the H750 and H900 alloys. At room temperature, the H900 alloy shows a yield and tensile strengths of 498 and 752 MPa, respectively, along with an elongation of 52.5%. The strengths are higher in the H750 alloy than in the H900 alloy, while the elongation is lower (28%). At cryogenic temperatures, the strengths and elongation are improved over the room-temperature values. In the H900 alloy, the yield strength, tensile strength and elongation are 698 MPa, 1,128 MPa and 78.6%, respectively, at cryogenic temperatures. Higher yield and tensile strengths (970 and 1,314 MPa) and lower elongation (46.3%) are also shown in the H750 alloy at cryogenic temperature.
